TITLE: Seeing the forest for the deer: Do reductions in deer-disturbance lead to forest recovery?
SPECIES: T1=Cervus nippon (deer); T2=Odocoileus virginianus (deer, White-tailed deer); T3=Populus tremuloides (trees); T4=Liriodendron tulipifera (tree); T5=Quercus rubra (Q. rubra, oak); T6=Canis lupus (wolves); T7=Quercus velutina (Q. velutina); T8=Acer saccharum (maple); T9=Carpinus caroliniana; T10=Cervus elaphus; T11=Fraxinus americana (ash); T12=Juglans nigra; T13=Ostrya virginiana; T14=Pinus strobus; T15=Prunus serotina; T16=Quercus alba (Q. alba); T17=Tilia americana
CONTEXT: Our objectives were to test whether: (i) prolonged periods of high deer browsing reduce canopy tree regeneration in Carolinian forest after 12-years of monitoring, and (ii) subsequent, intensive deer culling over 16-years restores earlier depleted tree size classes and deer-preferred species. Our study site is the largest remaining tract of the eastern deciduous (Carolinian) forest in Canada, and contains large tracts of Midwestern oak savanna, one of the world's most endangered ecosystems (North American distribution <0.02% of pre-European settlement). Rondeau Provincial Park, Ontario, Canada (3 254 ha, 42°17′N, 81°52′W) is situated on a cuspate sandspit extending out into Lake Erie with a north-south orientation consisting of sand dune ridges and seasonally-flooded sloughs. Species adapted to seasonal submersion in water, such as pumpkin, black, and red ash (Fraxinus profunda; F. nigra; F. pennsylvanica, respectively), and silver maple (Acer saccharinum), are primarily located within the sloughs, with the ridges comprised of American beech-hornbeam (Fagus grandifolia and Carpinus caroliniana, respectively) and sugar maple (Acer saccharum) stands with sparse red, black, and white oak (Quercus rubra, Q. velutina, and Q. alba, respectively), tulip tree (Liriodendron tulipifera), sassafras (Sassafras alba), white ash (Fraxinus americana), bitternut hickory (Carya cordiformis), black walnut (Juglans nigra) and American basswood (Tilia americana) (Figs. S1 and S2).
TEXT:
[1] (abs) High levels of deer browsing can prevent canopy tree regeneration, but little is known about changes to forest size-structure following long-term deer herd reductions.
[2] (abs) We monitored changes in forest stand structure and composition in southwestern Ontario, Canada, over 28-years using permanent plots.
[3] (abs) Our study site was the largest remaining tract of Carolinian (deciduous) forest in Canada (11 km2), a habitat type that contains up to a fifth of Canada's species at risk and is under intense anthropogenic pressures.
[4] (abs) We recorded declines in all tree size classes between 1981 and 1996, during which densities of whitetailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) reached a peak of 55 deer km-2.
[5] (abs) Despite significant and sustained deer herd reductions between 1996 and 2009, which reduced deer densities to 7 deer km-2, there was limited recruitment of small trees and declines in basal area of tree species that were sensitive to deer browsing.
[6] (abs) Our results suggest that recovery from herbivory is a protracted process during which canopy tree regeneration may continue to decline despite a reduction in browsing pressure due to deer culling.
[7] (abs) Large declines in canopy-tree densities in Carolinian forests may lead to forest size-structures and herbaceous plant communities that resemble rare oak savanna habitat, creating difficult decisions for conservation managers aiming to protect rare and endangered species within native ecosystems.
[8] (abs) We recommend that managers protect Carolinian forest stands and encourage canopy tree regeneration by increasing seed sources of native trees.
[9] (abs) While deer control is essential in reducing forest damage, our results highlight the need to explore other forms of active management to expedite otherwise slow increases in tree density.
[10] (res) Small trees (<6 cm DBH) were 72% less frequent within plots in 1996 after 19-years of >30 deer km-2 than in 1981 when deer densities first began to increase, leading to changes in forest size structure (D = 0.35, p < 0.001; Fig. 2A and B).
[11] (res) The loss of small trees was accompanied by an increase over time in mean basal area per individual (±standard error) across size classes (1981: $147 \pm 17$ cm2; $1996: 299 \pm 51$ cm2; $t{18}$ = 4.02, p < 0.001).
[12] (res) Although the total abundance of large trees (>20 cm DBH) declined within forest plots by 21% in 1996 compared to 1981, this reduction was much less than that for smaller size classes (<20 cm DBH) of 57% between years.
[13] (res) Reductions in small trees were mirrored by the significantly lower densities of saplings, but not adult trees (>7.5 cm DBH), within browsed plots in 1993 compared to adjacent exclosures ($\chi^2_2$ = 13.88, p < 0.001 and $\chi^2_2$ = 2.06, p = 0.357, respectively; Fig. 3).
[14] (res) Densities of small trees (<2 cm DBH) increased by 4.5 times between 1996 and 2009 following deer herd reductions, while small to mid-sized trees (2-12 cm DBH) declined by 41% during this period due to previously low abundances of small trees in 1996 that moved upwards through the forest canopy (D = 0.25, p < 0.001; Fig. 2B and C).
[15] (res) Large-sized trees (>40 cm DBH) declined in the forest size structure by 20 trees ha-1 between 1996 and 2009, and this was much greater than the reduction in density between 1981 and 1996 of 4 trees $ha^{-1}$, suggesting that the 1998 windstorm may have contributed to these reductions.
[16] (res) Despite the loss of large trees, mean basal area per individual (±standard error) within comparable plots did not change between 1996 and 2009 (1996: $298 \pm 60 \text{ cm}^2$; 2009: $257 \pm 39 \text{ cm}^2$; $t{15} = 0.92$, p = 0.371), in part due to the growth and increased abundance of smaller trees following deer herd reductions.
[17] (res) Understorey light availability measured 1-month prior to the 1998 windstorm event was not significantly different from light levels recorded 11 months afterwards (mean $\pm$ standard error: $3.8 \pm 0.8$ and 3.5 ± 1.0% PAR, respectively; final model including only the effect of exclosure treatment with and without effect of year: $\chi_4^2 = 4.00$, p = 0.406).
[18] (res) The lack of a change in understorey PAR suggests that the loss of large trees due to the windstorm did not affect canopy light interception, presumably since these individuals occurred at relatively low densities.
[19] (res) The continued decline of large trees did result in lower maximum tree height (±standard error) recorded in each plot in 2009 compared to 1981 (1981: 27.8 ± 1.0 m; 2009: $20.9 \pm 1.2 \text{ m}$; $t{31} = 22.27$, p < 0.001).
[20] (res) Seedling densities were also lower in 2009, despite deer culling, than when deer densities began to increase in 1981 ($t{14}$ = 4.53, p < 0.001; Fig. 3), but were still greater than in 1996, when no seedlings >50 cm in height were The densities of small trees within exclosures were more than four times greater than in forest plots, and larger size classes were more abundant within exclosures in 2009 (D = 0.33, p < 0.001; Fig. 2C and D).
[21] (res) The size-structure of the exclosures also differed from that within forest-plots in 1981, with greater densities of small and large (>20 cm DBH) trees within exclosures (D = 0.36, p < 0.001; Fig. 2).
[22] (res) Light levels were significantly greater outside of the exclosures due to lower tree densities (mean ± standard error: 3.2 ± 1.0 and 4.1 ± 0.8% PAR in exclosures and control plots, respectively; final model with only effect of exclosure treatment nested within exclosure site versus model with only exclosure site: v2 = 18.74, p < 0.001).
[23] (res) Fig. 3.
[24] (res) Mean densities $\pm$ standard error of saplings and adults in browsed-control plots (open bars) and exclosures (hatched bars) in 1993 (for each, n = 9), and seedlings in permanent forest plots in 1981 (light gray) and 2009 (dark gray).
[25] (res) Saplings were <7.5 cm diameter at 40-cm height and >40 cm in height, adults were >7.5 cm DBH, and seedlings were $\leq$ 1.4 m height irrespective of DBH.
[26] (res) Denotes significant differences ($\alpha$ = 0.05) between saplings in controls and exclosures, and seedlings in 1981 and 2009 (see text for details).

S1 and S2).
TEXT:
[27] (res) The composition of basal area within plots significantly differed over time (F2,47 = 0.86, p = 0.002).
[28] (res) Following deer herd reductions (1996–2009), virtually all plots increased along axis 1 and 2 of the ordination (14/16 and 15/16 plots, respectively), which were positively associated with a plot-level basal area comprised of species that increased in abundance in the presence of deer (correlation between V index and position of plots in ordination space: r 2 = 0.63, p = 0.029; n = 15).
[29] (res) Species that were presumably sensitive to deer browsing, and therefore, increased in abundance only within deer exclosures (V > 0), comprised less of the total basal area of plots in 2009 than in 1996.
[30] (res) There were no consistent temporal changes in within-plot composition along any axis between 1981 and 1996 and composition was unrelated to the water, shade, and drought tolerance of species across time periods (for all, r 2 < 0.29, p > 0.200).
[31] (res) Fig. 4.
[32] (res) Non-metric multidimensional scaling ordination of basal area with Bray-Curtis distance measures for 16 permanent forest plots at Rondeau Provincial Park, Ontario (stress = 13.97).
[33] (res) Black arrows indicate direction of change in plots from 1981 to 1996 and 1996 to 2009.
[34] (res) Twelve most common species are plotted: ACSC = Acer saccharum; CACA = Carpinus caroliniana; FRAM = Fraxinus americana; JUNI = Juglans nigra; LITU = Liriodendron tulipifera; OSVI = Ostrya virginiana; PIST = Pinus strobus; PRSE = Prunus serotina; QUAL = Quercus alba; QURU = Q. rubra; QUVE = Q. velutina; and TIAM = Tilia americana.
[35] (res) We also plotted the vector of species responses to deer exclusion (V, dark gray).
[36] (dis) Our study is among the first to demonstrate continued declines in canopy trees despite some understorey regeneration during intensive deer herd reductions.
[37] (dis) This finding suggests that culling alone may only reduce rather than eliminate the negative impacts of high deer densities (>10 deer km-2) on tree density and composition observed at our site and in many other temperate forests.
[38] (dis) Reductions in small trees associated with high deer densities can have cascading effects into larger size classes over time, leading to continual declines in canopy trees without any regeneration even when browse pressures are removed.
[39] (dis) Declines in canopy tree density that enlarge canopy gaps or reduce canopy tree height may further increase wind speeds, and thus act as a positive feedback to further increase the susceptibility of large-sized trees to windthrow.
[40] (dis) Similarly, declines in tree density that reduce lateral rooting mass, and hence soil stability, may further increase the susceptibility of trees to windthrow.
[41] (dis) Reductions in canopy-tree densities deplete seed sources and may strongly limit the potential for increased seedling and sapling densities following deer culling.
[42] (dis) We observed some recruitment of small trees within forest plots by 2009, suggesting that recovery from herbivory may be occurring but is an extremely protracted process.
[43] (dis) In New Zealand Nothofagus forests, reductions in deer densities over 44 years similarly led to small increases in the densities of deer-preferred tree seedlings and saplings.
[44] (dis) Hardwood species may require >10 years of deer exclusion in order for seedling recruitment to increase and in part, this ''legacy" of deer browsing may persist long after browse pressures are reduced because of depletion in seed sources.
[45] (dis) The establishment of species that respond positively to deer browsing may also result in shifts in community composition that persist once deer are removed; e.g. browse-tolerant and herbivore-avoided graminoids and ferns that form thick monocultures under high deer densities more effectively compete for light than tree seedlings and limit canopy tree regeneration.
[46] (dis) Once seedlings are able to establish, long periods may still be required to escape the browse layer, e.g. late successional conifers require >30 years of protection from deer browsing in order to reach higher size classes.
[47] (dis) These responses may arise because of highly non-linear relationships between deer densities and seedling regeneration, and the relatively slow growth of long-lived canopy tree species.
[48] (dis) Where forage is relatively uncommon, reductions in deer densities may not be accompanied by linear increases in seedling densities because deer may simply broaden their diets to include less-preferred forage (e.g. leaf litter) rather than avoid consuming live forage.
